title: Short Stuff: Why Spilling Salt is Unlucky
summary: Short Stuff episode on why spilling salt is considered unlucky and why people throw salt over the left shoulder. Josh and Chuck draw on a HowStuffWorks article by Debbie Ronkham. They cover the claim that salt was valuable and Roman soldiers were partly paid in salt (the origin of "salary"), Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper with salt spilled near Judas, salt as a symbol of purity and preservation in Christianity, Slavic and African folk tales about salt, Japanese use of salt for protection, and the left-shoulder toss tied to the devil sitting on one's left shoulder and the Latin root of "sinister." They close with a conjectural explanation that the ritual relieves anxiety and became a positive feedback loop.

segments.title: Opening and introduction to the article
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the Short Stuff episode, note that it is an old HowStuffWorks article by Debbie Ronkham, and pose the question of why spilling salt is bad luck and why people throw it over the left shoulder.

segments.title: Personal experiences with the salt superstition
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether they know the superstition. Josh says he throws salt over his left shoulder whenever he spills it, while Chuck says he has rarely seen people do it.

segments.title: Salary etymology and Roman soldiers
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the claim that 'salary' comes from salt, and that Roman soldiers were partly paid in salt or money to buy salt. They say it is ambiguous rather than fully true or fully a myth, and that salt's value is a likely origin of the bad luck belief.

segments.title: Last Supper painting and religious associations
segments.summary: Josh notes that Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper shows salt spilled near Judas, a possible religious link to bad luck. The hosts also note that Christianity treats salt as a symbol of holiness and purity, tied to its use in preserving food.

segments.title: Salt folklore: Slavic and African tales
segments.summary: Josh recounts a Slavic folk tale in which a father's youngest daughter compares her love to salt and is banished, later recognized as most loving. Chuck notes an African folk tale where salt stands for wisdom or life trials, so spilling it can signal misfortune or ignorance. The Last Supper salt spill is confirmed in the painting.

segments.title: Salt protection in Japan
segments.summary: Josh describes Japanese culture's use of salt to protect against bad luck and evil spirits, citing a personal example of a salt-filled prescription bottle his partner's mother kept in a glove compartment.

segments.title: Left shoulder, the devil, and the Latin word sinister
segments.summary: Chuck explains that the left-shoulder toss is an antidote, linked to the belief that the devil sits over the left shoulder and the spilled salt invites him. Josh adds that sinister is Latin for left, which explains the devil's placement, and mentions cartoon angel and devil imagery. Josh then proposes, as conjecture, that the toss relieves anxiety and created a positive feedback loop.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck jokes about spilling salt on purpose; Josh tells him not to. The hosts sign off and the iHeartRadio credit runs.
